entities.name: New York University
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
New York University (NYU), founded in 1831 in New York City by Albert Gallatin (former Secretary of the Treasury under Jefferson and Madison) with the explicit democratic vision that a great university should be open to students regardless of religious affiliation or social class — in contrast to elite colonial-era institutions — is one of the world's largest private research universities, with 60,000+ students and campuses in New York, Abu Dhabi, and Shanghai. NYU's urban identity and its location in Greenwich Village gave it a distinctive character: proximity to the arts, bohemian culture, and New York's intellectual life.

Gallatin's 1830 prospectus for NYU explicitly rejected religious tests and aristocratic admissions — the 19th-century American university democratization movement's founding document. NYU's Washington Square location (1837-present) placed it in the heart of Greenwich Village, which became the epicenter of American counterculture: NYU hosted or trained Dylan Thomas, Jackson Pollock, Henry James, Walt Whitman, and Martin Scorsese. The Stern School of Business (1900) and Tisch School of the Arts (1965) made NYU leaders in business education and film/performing arts.

NYU's global university model — establishing fully functioning overseas campuses (Abu Dhabi 2010, Shanghai 2012) rather than satellite offices — pioneered the 'global network university' concept, creating the first university to grant NYU degrees at three degree-granting campuses on three continents. The NYU Law School and Medical School are consistently ranked among America's top 10. NYU's 60,000+ enrollment in Manhattan makes it the nation's largest private university and one of its largest landowners in Lower Manhattan.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: NYU — founded on explicit democratic non-sectarian principles by Gallatin — pioneered the American urban research university model and, with its Abu Dhabi and Shanghai campuses, the 21st-century global network university concept, making it one of the most consequential architectural models for higher education globally.
